new_statements.quote: 52. L'accent ne porte sur les préfixes et les suffixes qu'autant qu'on veut attirer sur eux l'attention. En règle générale l'accent porte sur la voyelle longue du radical quelle que soit la place que celle-ci occupe, et, quand il n'y a pas de voyelle longue, c'est la première syllabe que l'on accentue. Dans les verbes qui se terminent par une consonne, l'accent porte toujours sur la dernière syllabe. La première voyelle du pluriel emphatique (gini, gin) est toujours longue et accentuée.
new_statements.translation: 52. The accent falls on prefixes and suffixes only insofar as one wishes to draw attention to them. As a general rule the accent falls on the long vowel of the radical, whatever position it occupies, and, when there is no long vowel, it is the first syllable that is accented. In verbs ending in a consonant, the accent always falls on the last syllable. The first vowel of the emphatic plural (gini, gin) is always long and accented.
new_statements.citation: Haumonté, J.-D., J. Parisot & Lucien Adam. 1882. Grammaire et vocabulaire de la langue taensa, avec textes traduits et commentés. (Bibliothèque linguistique américaine, IX.) Paris: Maisonneuve.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the (forged) grammar: stress targets the long vowel of the root regardless of position; roots without a long vowel take initial stress; affixes are unstressed unless emphasized; consonant-final verbs are said to stress the final syllable. CAVEAT: the language is an 1880s fabrication; this rule describes no real speech.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; 'light' accent on the passive index vowel (except in the infinitive) and on the vowel preceding final -ao/-aou diphthongs (p. 2); in 'expletive pronouns' the simple pronoun is accented first and the first vowel of the suffixed particle second (p. 32).
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant-final verbs: final-syllable accent per p. 32, but p. 21 (Ch. VI) says 'Les verbes terminés par une consonne ont l'accent sur la seconde syllabe' -- the grammar contradicts itself. Emphatic plural gini/gin and medial vowels of emphatic pronouns always long and accented.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word (radical plus affixes); no phrase-level discussion. The entire description is of a fictitious language (Brinton 1885/1890; Swanton 1908), so the statement has no empirical referent; the real Taensa spoke Natchez (natc1249).
new_statements.identity_note: taen1234 is a retired Glottolog Bookkeeping entry ('based on a misunderstanding'); its sole Glottolog's most extensive description is Haumonte, Parisot & Adam 1882, a grammar of an invented language exposed as a forgery by Brinton (1885; Essays 1890 pp. 452-467) and Swanton (1908, Am. Anthropologist 10: 32: 'the language derived from or through M. Parisot is not Taensa, and was probably never spoken by any people whatsoever'). ASJP marks its TAENSA list 'Oth.FAKE / Spurious'. The historical Taensa of Louisiana spoke Natchez or a close variety (natc1249, Natchez), for which no independent Taensa linguistic data survive. The accent statement quoted below therefore describes a fictitious language and must not be catalogued as a description of any real speech variety.

sources.locator: Grammaire, Chapitre VII 'Accent', §52, p. 32 (PDF p. 64 of the JCB scan); cf. p. 21 and p. 2
sources.note: Ch. VII 'Accent' §52, p. 32: accent falls on the long vowel of the radical wherever it is; if no long vowel, on the first syllable; prefixes/suffixes unaccented unless emphasized; consonant-final verbs accent the last syllable (but p. 21 says such verbs accent the SECOND syllable -- internally inconsistent). p. 2: i, u long when accented. The whole language is a documented forgery.
